newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan inflation seen up despite price freeze.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan inflation seen up despite price freeze.

text.p: Pakistan's inflation is likely to edge higher over the next few months even though the new government has frozen fuel prices and utility charges until June, analysts said on Wednesday.
Jahanzeb Naseer, head of research at Jardine Fleming Pakistan, said the freeze was unlikely to dent inflationary pressure in the last four months of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).

"Our CPI (consumer price index) target for the year ending June 30 was 12.6 percent on a 12-month moving average. If we incorporate the price freeze, the figure comes down to 12.4 percent," Naseer said. The year-on-year CPI figure would be somewhere close to 16.7 percent, he predicted.
The consumer price index increased 13.83 percent year-on-year in February, while the 12-month moving average rose 11.10 percent, the Federal Bureau of Statistics said on Tuesday.
The wholesale price index rose 15.67 percent year-on-year, while the 12-month moving average went up 12.26 percent.
Consumer prices gained 1.09 percent over January and wholesale prices 0.65 percent.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif announced soon after winning the February 3 election that fuel prices and utility charges would be not be increased before the end of the fiscal year.
Naseer said the price freeze would start showing in March or April inflation figures, but sharp price rises in December and January would keep inflation high for the rest of the year.
He attributed February's fuel and food price increases to higher consumption in the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
The chief economist at a foreign bank said shortages of essential food items such as wheat and sugar and surges in prices of imported fuel had pushed up other prices.
"The 34.7 percent increase in the price of high speed diesel since February 13, 1996, is primarily responsible for the increase in prices of transportation since January 1996.

"Furthermore, the 89.5 percent increase in the price of furnace oil, the main input in thermal power plants, over the same period is correspondingly responsible for the rise in the fuel/lighting sub-index of the CPI," he said.
Transport and communication prices rose 16.3 percent year-on-year in February, the highest single increase. Fuel and lighting went up 15.78 percent and food 15.27 percent.
The economist, who asked not to be named, said the price freeze was a short-term strategy to deal with the political implications of high inflation.

"But the measure is likely to increase distortions in the economy. Freezing utility prices in the face of high fuel prices will result in government subsidies and drain government revenues that are already short of targets," he said.
He said revenue collection in February was 20 billion rupees against a target of 36 billion. "If the trend continues we are looking at a 23 to 24 percent drop in revenues," he added.
The government has not announced official figures for monthly revenue collection.
Naseer said inflationary pressure could prompt further tightening of credit expansion which would stifle economic growth.
"A 10 to 11 percent devaluation post-June is possible if the CPI 12-month moving average surges above 12 percent," he said.
